claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units only moderately.
The best policy is to strengthen tenure security and add a light band on initial rents.
A hard cap on rent levels would backfire.
Tenants face serious harms, including high rent burden and insecurity.
Mr Chan pays HK$5,800 for 120 square feet, about a third of household income.
Mrs Wong has lived in a subdivided unit for nine years with no written agreement.
Real rent burden for SDU households worsened from 31 to 34 percent even after the 2021 ordinance.
Landlords say a hard cap is confiscatory and they will convert or empty units.
The landlords' exit threat is not proven because its evidence is weak.
A binding cap would reduce marginal SDU-type stock by roughly 3 to 5 percent over five years.
A 15 percent cut in initial rents would transfer about HK$900 per month to incumbents but block 3,000 to 4,000 households per year.
Berlin shows that caps protect those already inside while harming those still outside.
Enforcement capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year.
A band-based cap requires a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years.
Enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tenants, such as those without written agreements.
A hard cap framed as deprivation of income would invite compensation claims and judicial review.
A light band on initial rents with three-year tenure security protects tenants while keeping landlords in the market.
The landlords' exit threat should be taken seriously but not accepted at face value.
Policy should be reviewed with better data because current figures are partly extrapolated.

cites.sentence: Mr Chan pays HK$5,800 for 120 square feet, roughly a third of household income, and describes insecurity as worse than price: his landlord ended a tenancy with two weeks' notice when he asked for a window repair [D3p1].
Mrs Wong has lived in an SDU for nine years with no written agreement, and reports that the 2021 ordinance changed nothing she can see [D4p1].
Real rent burden for SDU households worsened from 31 to 34 percent even after the ordinance [D2p2].
The landlords association says a hard cap is confiscatory and that members will convert or empty units if returns fall below mortgage cost [D5p1]
The association admits it has no data on members' actual margins, and its cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate [D5p3].
The reviewed elasticity estimates for marginal SDU-type stock run 0.31 to 0.48: a 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].

The modelled Hong Kong scenario is starker: a 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about HK$900 per month to incumbents, against 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].

Berlin illustrates the mechanism in practice: capped initial-offer rents fell, listing supply contracted within a year as owners withheld or rerouted flats, and when the law was struck down a backlog of suppressed increases released above the pre-cap trend [D7p1][D7p2].

Berlin illustrates the mechanism in practice: capped initial-offer rents fell, listing supply contracted within a year as owners withheld or rerouted flats, and when the law was struck down a backlog of suppressed increases released above the pre-cap trend [D7p1][D7p2].
The Berlin lesson is explicit: the cap protects those already inside, and the bill is handed to those still outside [D7p3].
First, enforcement capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based cap requires a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1].

Second, the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, Mrs Wong's situation [D4p1], or the newest arrivals, so enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail [D10p2].
